strengths: Original and practically useful idea: rather than accelerating the proof of optimality (as in most ML-for-MIP work), the paper learns to exploit the well-known gap between finding and proving optimal solutions, using conformal prediction to give a statistical stopping rule with finite-sample guarantees. This reframing (Section 3, Figure 1) is a clean and compelling motivation.

The theoretical development is fairly complete: precise problem formalization (parametric MIPs, true vs. algorithmic gap, deterministic vs. probabilistic stopping times), a conformal calibration procedure (Theorem 4.1) with a full proof via exchangeability, and additional sample-conditional guarantees (Theorems 5.1, 5.2) that go beyond marginal coverage, which is a nice extra layer of rigor connecting to recent conformal-prediction theory (Duchi, 2025; Vovk, 2012).

Reasonably broad empirical validation across six problem families from Distributional MIPLIB, two different solvers (Gurobi and COPT), and several naive baselines (stopping at 1st/3rd incumbent). Reported speedups are large (60-95%) in most families, and the paper transparently reports a family (GISP) where the method offers little benefit, along with a forthright discussion of limitations (training cost, distribution-shift assumption, problem-dependent gains).

The paper is generally clearly written, with a good diagram (Figure 2) and figure (Figure 1) that intuitively convey the mechanism, and the pipeline (train/calibrate/deploy) is described in enough detail to be conceptually reproducible.
weaknesses: Internal inconsistency in the central theoretical result: Theorem 4.1 as stated concludes P[gθc+1(τ̂κ(θc+1)) ≤ ϵ] ≥ n/(c+1), but the proof (via Lemma 4.2, applied with parameter n) actually derives ≥ (n+1)/(c+1), and the subsequent 'apply the theorem' paragraph and Theorem 5.2's proof both use (n+1)/(c+1). This off-by-one discrepancy between the theorem statement and its own proof is not reconciled anywhere and undermines confidence in the precise correctness of the flagship guarantee.

The empirical coverage substantially violates the claimed 95% guarantee in several settings (e.g., OTS/CP-COPT: 78.6% correct, MMCN/CP-COPT: 80.0%, GISP/CP-COPT: 85.0%, MVC/CP-GRB: 88.0%, MIS/CP-COPT: 91.0%; see Table in Appendix A), yet the paper never explicitly discusses these shortfalls in the main text, nor connects them quantitatively to the finite-sample slack allowed by Theorem 5.2 (which could explain but does not obviously fully justify gaps of 15-20 percentage points, especially for larger calibration sets like c=100). This is a serious gap for a paper whose central selling point is a 'rigorous probabilistic guarantee.'

Experimental protocol choices may inflate the apparent benefit: presolve is disabled and only a single thread is used for both the baseline and the proposed method. Disabling presolve is atypical for practical MIP solving and can substantially slow down baseline solvers, potentially exaggerating relative speedups; this choice is not justified or ablated.

Minor but noticeable inconsistencies: the abstract states results are from 'five problem families,' while Section 6 and Table 1 present six (CFLP, GISP, OTS, MMCNDP, MIS, MVC); the MMCN family is also referred to inconsistently ('MMCNDP' in Table 1 vs. 'MMCN-medium-BI' in Table 2/text).

Limited baselines: comparisons are only against exact-solver default termination and two trivial stop-at-k-solutions heuristics; there is no comparison to other plausible early-stopping or ML-guided termination strategies (e.g., simple gap-extrapolation rules, other predictors besides LSTM, or non-conformal calibration baselines), making it hard to assess how much of the benefit comes from conformal calibration per se versus the predictor architecture.

Practical overhead of running the LSTM predictor as part of a solver callback (inference cost per callback, frequency of calls) is not discussed or included in reported solve times, and the substantial upfront cost of generating training data (solving 800 instances per family, some to the 600s cap) is only qualitatively acknowledged as a limitation rather than quantified.

strengths: The core idea—learning to predict the true (unknown) optimality gap from solver state and calibrating a stopping threshold via conformal prediction—is a clean and well-motivated reframing of the early-termination problem for branch-and-bound, clearly illustrated in Figure 1.

The paper provides a full theoretical pipeline: a finite-sample coverage theorem (4.1) built on a rolling-minimum/left-inverse construction to handle monotonicity, plus additional sample-conditional guarantees (Theorems 5.1, 5.2) on expected suboptimality/runtime and conditional success probability, which go beyond a bare marginal conformal guarantee.

Experiments span six MIP problem families (CFLP, GISP, OTS, MMCNDP, MIS, MVC) and two independent solvers (Gurobi, COPT), reporting consistent metrics (suboptimality, solve time, nodes, success rate) with reasonably thorough tabulated results in the appendix.

Reported speedups are large on most families (60-95%), and the idea of terminating MIP solves based on a learned proxy rather than improving in-solver decisions is a distinct angle relative to the dominant branching/cutting-plane learning literature.
weaknesses: Central soundness concern: the method's own reported 'Correct' (empirical coverage) rates fall substantially below the nominal 1-α=95% guarantee in multiple settings (e.g., CP-COPT on OTS: 78.6%, CP-COPT on MMCN: 80.0%, CP-COPT on GISP: 85.0%). With test-set sizes of 72-100 instances, these deviations are too large to be explained by sampling noise alone, yet the paper does not diagnose or discuss this violation beyond a generic one-line remark that the method 'may not solve all problems' due to the probabilistic guarantee — this undercuts the paper's primary selling point (rigorous probabilistic guarantees on solution quality).

The calibration sets are very small for some families (e.g., OTS uses c=28), which is too coarse to reliably target a 95% quantile (requiring roughly n≈26-27 out of 28), yet no sensitivity analysis or discussion of how calibration-set size affects guarantee reliability is provided.

Notational inconsistencies undermine rigor and readability: Section 4.2 redefines gθ(t) as the predictor's output (overloading the symbol already used in Section 3 for the true, unknown gap), and the loss in Eq. (4)/preceding display drops the θ subscript/hat notation (g(Xθ(t)) vs ĝθ(t)), making it unclear exactly what is being learned and fit. Theorem 4.1's stated bound (n/(c+1)) does not match the bound actually derived and used in the text immediately after the proof ((n+1)/(c+1)), which is confusing even if not technically incorrect.

The theoretical contribution is largely a direct application of standard split-conformal/quantile machinery (and existing VC and DKW-type bounds from Mohri et al. and Vovk) to a new setting, with the main technical addition being the left-inverse/rolling-minimum trick to handle the fact that gθ(t) is not observed directly; this is a solid but incremental theoretical step rather than a major methodological advance.

The assumption that 'θ and t uniquely identify the algorithm state' (Section 3.2) is a strong idealization of real branch-and-bound dynamics (which are affected by numerical and implementation-level stochasticity even on fixed hardware), and this assumption is never empirically tested or discussed as a source of potential guarantee violation, despite being foundational to transferring per-instance determinism into the conformal argument.

Reproducibility is weak: the manuscript includes an empty/placeholder code link ('Code for our experiments is available through the following link:' with no URL), and there is no appendix detailing network architecture training specifics beyond brief mentions, hyperparameters for the squashing function, or how Lθ(t)/Uθ(t) bounds for φ were chosen, making independent replication difficult.

The abstract claims results on 'five problem families' while the experiments and tables present six, an inconsistency that suggests insufficient proofreading and raises minor doubts about the care taken in finalizing reported results.

The chosen baselines (terminating after 1 or 3 feasible solutions) are weak straw-man comparators with no calibration or guarantee, which inflates the apparent advantage of the proposed method; a more informative comparison would include simpler statistical/heuristic early-stopping rules (e.g., fixed time budgets per family, or naive extrapolation of the bound gap) to isolate the specific value added by the learned predictor versus the conformal calibration step itself.

No analysis is given of the learned predictor's accuracy in isolation (e.g., calibration plots of predicted vs. true gap, error distributions across time), making it hard to assess whether reported speedups stem from a genuinely informative predictor or from the generous slack built into the conformal threshold at the chosen α.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated idea: exploiting the empirical gap between when branch-and-bound finds an optimal/near-optimal solution and when it can prove optimality, which is a practically important but underexplored angle relative to the dominant line of work that tries to speed up the proof itself.

Rigorous theoretical treatment: the paper not only gives a marginal coverage guarantee via a split-conformal-style argument (Theorem 4.1) but also derives stronger sample-conditional guarantees on expected suboptimality/runtime (Theorem 5.1, via VC-dimension arguments) and on the conditional success probability (Theorem 5.2, via Vovk's result), which goes beyond the typical marginal-only guarantees seen in most conformal prediction applications papers.

Reasonably broad empirical evaluation across six problem families from distributional MIPLIB, with two different solvers (Gurobi and COPT), several weak baselines, and multiple reported metrics (suboptimality, solve time, number of nodes, percent correctly solved), giving a fairly complete picture of behavior.

The paper is clearly written, with a good illustrative figure (Fig. 1) motivating the core observation, and a clean method diagram (Fig. 2) that aids understanding of the training/calibration/deployment pipeline.
Reported speedups are substantial (60–95% on most families) while maintaining low suboptimality, suggesting the method could have real practical value for time-critical repeated-solve settings.
The limitations section is honest, acknowledging the offline training cost, the problem-dependence of achievable speedup, and the i.i.d./distribution-shift assumption underlying the guarantee.
weaknesses: The abstract claims results on 'five problem families' but the experiments (Table 1, Appendix A) list six (CFLP, GISP, OTS, MMCNDP, MIS, MVC); this inconsistency should be fixed and may indicate incomplete proofreading elsewhere.

In several experiments the empirical 'Correct' percentage for the conformal method falls noticeably below the nominal 1-α = 95% target (e.g., 85% and 78.6% for GISP/OTS with CP COPT, 80% for MMCN), which is not discussed in the main text despite being a central claim of the paper (rigorous 95% guarantee). While consistent with the theory (a single calibration draw can undershoot, especially with small c, e.g., c=28 for OTS), the paper should explicitly discuss this empirical under-coverage and its practical implications, since a user relying on the stated guarantee may be misled by headline numbers.

The core conformal-calibration result (Theorem 4.1) is a relatively direct adaptation of standard split/full conformal quantile arguments (closely following Lemma 4.2, essentially a standard conformal exchangeability argument) to the early-stopping setting; the technical novelty is mostly in the problem formulation and bookkeeping (left-inverses, rolling minima) rather than in fundamentally new conformal machinery.

The baseline comparisons (stopping after 1 or 3 incumbent solutions) are quite weak straw-man baselines with extremely poor suboptimality (often >50-200%), and the paper does not compare against more competitive learned-stopping or heuristic-gap-threshold baselines (e.g., a simple tuned relative-gap cutoff, or the related hierarchical learning approach of Clarke & Stellato (2025) cited in related work), making it hard to assess how much of the benefit comes from the conformal calibration specifically versus simply any early termination.

No ablations are provided for key design choices (LSTM architecture, choice of covariates, the inverse-weighting scheme in Eq. 5, sensitivity to calibration set size c), limiting insight into what drives the reported performance and reproducibility of design decisions.
The code availability link in the paper is left blank ('Code for our experiments is available through the following link:'), which undermines reproducibility at submission time.

The offline cost of generating training data (solving d=800 instances per family with full callback logging) is not quantified in wall-clock terms or compared against the amortized savings, so it is unclear how many deployment solves are needed before the upfront training cost is recouped.

The method's guarantee fundamentally requires i.i.d. draws from a fixed distribution of 'similar' instances, which is a real restriction for many practical MIP use cases where instance distributions drift or are not well-defined in advance; this is appropriately flagged as a limitation but could be explored further empirically (e.g., a controlled distribution-shift experiment).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: exploits the well-known gap between finding an optimal solution and proving its optimality in branch-and-bound, illustrated concretely in Figure 1.

Rigorous theoretical contribution: Theorem 4.1 correctly adapts split conformal prediction (via left-inverse functions and a rolling-minimum trick to enforce monotonicity) to the time-indexed stopping problem, with a clean proof building on a standard exchangeability lemma.

Goes beyond marginal coverage to provide sample-conditional guarantees (Theorem 5.2), expected suboptimality/runtime bounds via VC-dimension arguments (Theorem 5.1), and robustness to distribution shift in TV distance (Theorem 5.3), which meaningfully strengthens the practical relevance of the guarantee.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across six diverse problem families (including two real-world datasets, OTS and MMCN) with two different solvers (Gurobi, COPT), showing consistent, often large (60-95%) speedups while empirically respecting the stated coverage target.

Thorough appendix experiments: ablations against simpler predictors (linear model, upper-bound-rate heuristic), standalone SCIP primal heuristics, additional Gurobi tolerance levels, and sensitivity analyses to distribution shift and calibration set size, which substantiate that the LSTM predictor is learning nontrivial, useful signal rather than a trivial pattern.

The remark on avoiding multiple-testing issues by calibrating a single threshold prior to deployment is a nice, clearly explained methodological point that distinguishes the approach from a naive repeated-testing scheme.
Honest discussion of limitations (added training/data-generation cost, problem-dependent speedup, reliance on distributional assumption) without overselling the method.
weaknesses: The core theoretical machinery is essentially a direct, if careful, application of standard split conformal prediction (quantile-based calibration and finite-sample marginal coverage); the technical novelty lies mainly in adapting it to a time-indexed stopping rule rather than in fundamentally new conformal theory.

Some baselines (GRB1/GRB3/COPT1/COPT3, terminating after 1 or 3 incumbents) are weak strawmen with extremely poor suboptimality (often >50-200%), which may inflate the apparent advantage of the proposed method relative to the main text figures; the more informative comparison against Gurobi/COPT at looser MIPGap tolerances is relegated to an appendix.

For the real-world families (OTS-medium, MMCN-medium-BI), the calibration and test sets are small (e.g., c=28, l=72 for OTS) because only 100 real instances exist, which limits the statistical reliability of the empirical coverage estimates on exactly the datasets meant to demonstrate practical applicability.

The method requires solving hundreds of full instances from the target distribution merely to generate training trajectories (state, gap over time), which is a substantial offline cost that is acknowledged but not deeply quantified (e.g., total wall-clock overhead of data generation and training is not clearly reported relative to the deployment-time savings).

No direct empirical comparison to other closely related learned-early-termination/predict-and-search approaches mentioned in related work (e.g., Apollo-MILP), only a conceptual distinction is provided, making it hard to gauge relative practical benefit against the most relevant recent learning-based baselines.

The predictor architecture (2-layer LSTM + MLP) and covariate choices are reasonable but fairly simple; the paper acknowledges this is swappable, but no evidence is given for how a stronger architecture (e.g., incorporating problem structure via GNNs) would change results, leaving open whether reported gains are near a ceiling or could be substantially improved.

strengths: The paper provides a rigorous theoretical foundation: Theorem 4.1 gives a clean split-conformal-style marginal coverage guarantee for a learned stopping time, and the paper goes further to establish sample-conditional guarantees (Theorems 5.1, 5.2) and robustness to distribution shift (Theorem 5.3), with complete, mostly careful proofs.

The 'multiple testing' remark correctly explains why a single pre-calibrated threshold avoids the usual sequential-testing inflation of error probability, which is a subtle but important point that is often mishandled in similar online-stopping settings.

Experiments span six diverse problem families (including two from real-world data) and two different solvers (Gurobi, COPT), with substantial additional material in the appendix: SCIP heuristic baselines, simple linear/heuristic predictor ablations, a sweep over standard solver MIPGap tolerances, and sensitivity analyses to distribution shift and calibration-set size. This breadth is unusually thorough for a paper of this scope.

The core empirical finding (large solve-time reductions while nominal ϵ-optimality coverage is approximately maintained, as shown in Figures 3-4 and Tables 5-10) is consistent across most families and is a clear, useful demonstration of the practical relevance of the method.
The paper is honest about its limitations (training cost, variable speedup across families such as GISP, and dependence on the i.i.d./bounded-TV-shift assumption), which strengthens its credibility.
weaknesses: The ablation in Appendix C (Tables 11-12) shows that a simple linear model (and even a trivial 'change in upper bound over 5s' heuristic) often matches or outperforms the LSTM predictor in both suboptimality and solve time (e.g., CFLP: linear gets 0.003% suboptimality vs. 0.018% for the LSTM, with comparable or better time). This undercuts the implicit motivating claim that a more complex learned model is needed to detect meaningful convergence patterns, and the paper does not adequately explain or address this result in the main text.

All experiments disable solver presolve and multithreading and fix MIPFocus=1, which are atypical settings for practical MIP deployment. This design choice likely exaggerates the apparent benefit of early stopping relative to a fully tuned, default solver configuration, limiting the practical significance of the reported speedups.

The magnitude of improvement varies widely across families (8% on GISP vs. >60-95% on others), and the paper offers only a post-hoc qualitative explanation (gap closes quickly after a good solution is found) without deeper analysis of what structural properties predict when the method will or will not help, limiting the generality of the claimed contribution.

For the OTS family, only c=28 calibration points are available, which is quite small relative to the theoretical O(1/√c) concentration terms in Theorems 5.1-5.2; the practical tightness of the stated guarantees in this low-data regime is not empirically scrutinized (e.g., no explicit numerical bound evaluation is shown for this setting).

There is a notational/implementation inconsistency between the theoretically defined, normalized optimality gap g_θ(t) = (U_θ(t)-z*(θ))/|z*(θ)| used throughout the theory (Sections 3-5) and the predictor target used in training (Section 4.2), which regresses on the unnormalized quantity U_θ(t)-z*(θ) with bounds [L_θ(t),U_θ(t)]; the paper does not clearly reconcile this discrepancy, leaving some ambiguity about exact correspondence between the trained model and the theorem's guarantees.

The method fundamentally requires fully solving many training instances from the target distribution to collect solver-state trajectories and the true optimal value z*(θ), which can be as expensive as the problem it purports to accelerate; while acknowledged as a limitation, the paper does not quantify this upfront cost relative to the downstream savings (e.g., total training+calibration time vs. aggregate test-time savings), making it hard to assess net practical benefit.

strengths: Clear and compelling motivation: formalizes and exploits the well-known but underused observation that branch-and-bound often finds the optimal solution long before it can certify optimality (nicely illustrated in Figure 1).

Sound theoretical contribution: the conformal calibration procedure (Theorem 4.1) gives a rigorous, distribution-free marginal guarantee on returned solution quality, and the paper goes further to provide sample-conditional guarantees on expected suboptimality/runtime (Theorem 5.1), conditional success probability concentration (Theorem 5.2), and robustness to bounded distribution shift (Theorem 5.3) -- this is a more complete theoretical treatment than typical split-conformal applications.

The 'multiple testing' remark is an important and often-overlooked subtlety; the paper correctly explains why a single pre-calibrated threshold avoids the inflated false-positive risk of naively checking a learned gap at every solver callback.

Thorough empirical evaluation across six diverse MIP families (two from real-world data) and two solvers (Gurobi, COPT), reporting suboptimality, solve time, node counts, and percent solved to tolerance, with substantial reported speedups (60%+ on 5/6 families).

Useful ablations: comparison to simpler predictors (linear model, UB-rate heuristic), SCIP primal heuristics, a range of standard ε-optimality tolerances, and sensitivity analyses to calibration-set size and distribution shift, which strengthen the credibility of the empirical claims and contextualize when the learned predictor adds value over naive heuristics.
Honest limitations section that acknowledges the expensive data-generation step, variable speedup across problem families (e.g., only 8% on GISP), and the assumption of distributional stability.
weaknesses: The appendix sensitivity analysis (Table 16) shows that for small calibration sets (e.g., c=5), empirical coverage can fall well below the nominal 1-α target (80% vs. 95%) with high variance, indicating the method's practical reliability is sensitive to calibration-set size in ways that could matter for problem families where only limited calibration data is available (e.g., OTS-medium with c=28), yet this caveat is not foregrounded in the main text.

Some baselines (GRB1, GRB3, COPT1, COPT3, stopping after 1 or 3 feasible solutions) are quite weak strawmen that trivially have poor suboptimality; a more informative comparison might include other adaptive/statistical early-stopping heuristics from the literature to better isolate the specific benefit of the conformal calibration versus simply using a learned or heuristic gap estimate with an ad hoc threshold.

The core conformal guarantee (Theorem 4.1) is a relatively direct instantiation of standard split-conformal/quantile exchangeability arguments (Lemma 4.2 essentially restates a well-known order-statistics coverage result); the technical novelty lies primarily in the problem formulation and the stopping-time construction rather than in new conformal methodology.

Reported speedups vary substantially by problem family (8% to 95%), and the paper does not provide much insight or diagnostic tooling for predicting a priori when the method will or will not be effective beyond the general comment that the finding/proving gap is problem-dependent.
The code repository link in Section 6.1 is left blank/incomplete in the submitted manuscript, which is a reproducibility concern (even if this is only an anonymization or formatting oversight).

The method still requires solving many representative instances from the target distribution to generate training trajectories, which can be computationally expensive and is acknowledged but not quantified (e.g., total wall-clock cost of the training-data generation phase relative to the savings obtained).
